doc.title: Slide Hampton interviewed by Monk Rowe, West Orange, New Jersey, July 30, 2003

title: Big band versus small group and what the big band teaches
summary: Hampton says the greats grew up in big bands; ensemble playing teaches harmony and resolutions he used when playing Dizzy's arrangements.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: Well you have done both small group and big band music. Is there a place that you’re most comfortable in? © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

You know you’re thinking — of course I’ve been asked that question many times and most musicians are. But see the thing is that we actually were raised in the big band period. And all the musicians that you hear playing the small groups that we aspired to, like Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie and Benny Goodman, Stan Getz, they all were raised in the big band period. And that was what prepared them so well to be so well presented in small groups, that big band experience. So actually we find both of them as important, but of course you can enjoy yourself in one way in a small group because you get to improvise more. And in the big band you have the wonderful experience of playing in the ensemble with other people, which is very important and wonderful also.
It might seem obvious to musicians what that positive experience of being in a big band is, but maybe for non-musicians who might see this tape, can you relate what kind of things you gain from that?

Well you know what people think when they see a person in a big group, they think that it is a kind of a situation that’s so well organized that it would kind of prevent you from being free enough to improvise. It’s not the case at all. Actually because improvisation is certainly a free style of playing music, but there is a lot of organization that goes on in an improvisation. To have a good improvisation there’s a composition that goes on, a certain amount of theory, a certain amount of all the things that you actually learned also in the large ensembles.
Hearing your note in place with everything else, I mean really helps your ear doesn’t it?

It does. And you hear the resolutions of the harmony, harmony of arrangements that are written by great arrangers. I remember when I played with the Dizzy Gillespie group and I was playing arrangements by Quincy Jones, by Dizzy himself, Ernie Wilkins, Melba Liston, Benny Golson. You learn about resolutions in the big group, because you hear all these resolving harmonies and things. So when you improvise you also use resolutions as a big part of the way that you make an improvisation.
